title: Signature Renewed Foliot Escapement
body:
Specifications

An original Signature design that renews the foliot idea with a balanced crossbar and sliding brass weights on a graduated scale, so the rate can be read off the bar rather than guessed. The crown wheel has 15 teeth and the verge carries pallets at right angles, sized for a longcase movement with a one-second beat. This is a Signature original, not a historical foliot, and it is labelled signature-original throughout.

Mechanism

The crown wheel drives the verge exactly as in the early form, but the foliot bar is balanced on a jewelled pivot and its weights lock with thumb screws, so the bar cannot slip in service. Each pallet releases one tooth per swing, and the graduated scale lets the owner return to a known rate after cleaning. The wide swing is kept deliberately, as a teaching display of how early timekeeping worked.

Maintenance

Keep the crown wheel clean, oil the verge pivots only, and check the thumb screws at every service, because a slipped weight changes the rate by minutes a day. Never oil the foliot bar itself, and never force the bar while the weights drive the train.

Build and restoration guidance

Build the bar from brass with steel weight sleeves, balance it before fitting the weights, and cut the crown wheel teeth to match the pallet spacing exactly. Test over a week, moving the weights one scale mark at a time, and record the rate at each mark.

Tools

Brass bar stock, thumb screws, clock oil, loupe, and a timing reference.

title: Signature Balanced Anchor Escapement
body:
Specifications

An original Signature anchor design with a counterweighted anchor and pallets faced with polished steel, made for a longcase clock with a seconds pendulum. The anchor spans a 30-tooth escape wheel, and the counterweight reduces the anchor's own effect on the pendulum. This is a Signature original design, labelled signature-original.

Mechanism

The anchor works on the recoil principle, but the counterweight is set so the anchor's mass is balanced about its pivot, which reduces the recoil's drag on the pendulum. One pallet locks while the other gives impulse, and the crutch fork drives the pendulum through a suspension spring. The tick is even when the counterweight is set correctly.

Maintenance

Oil the pallet faces with one tiny drop each and check the counterweight screw at every service. If the tick becomes uneven after cleaning, recheck the beat before touching the pallets, because beat errors are more common than pallet faults.

Build and restoration guidance

Build the anchor with the counterweight adjustable, set the pallet depths equally, and test the recoil by watching the seconds hand: a slight step back at each beat is normal for this design. File the pallets only as a pair, never one alone.

Tools

Anchor stock, counterweight, clock oil, beat tester, and screwdrivers.

title: Signature Silent Deadbeat Escapement
body:
Specifications

An original Signature deadbeat design with pallets faced in polished synthetic ruby and an escape wheel with 30 teeth, built for a quiet regulator clock. The locking faces are cut on a circle concentric with the wheel, so there is no recoil, and the impulse faces are polished to reduce the click. This is a Signature original, labelled signature-original.

Mechanism

A tooth locks on the pallet's locking face while the pendulum swings freely, then slides onto the impulse face to give the push, exactly on the deadbeat principle. The ruby faces reduce friction and wear, and the light anchor keeps the pendulum's swing undisturbed. Lock and drop are separate, so the pendulum's free arc is preserved.

Maintenance

Oil the impulse faces with the smallest drop and keep the ruby faces clean and free of dust. Never use abrasive polish on the ruby faces, and check the drop on both pallets at every service, because unequal drop makes the clock run unevenly.

Build and restoration guidance

Build the pallets as a matched pair, set the lock shallow and equal, and test at a two-degree arc, where this design is at its best. Record the drop on each pallet in the service notes so the next service can compare.

Tools

Ruby pallet blanks, pallet setter, clock oil, loupe, and timing machine.

title: Signature Hopping Grasshopper Escapement
body:
Specifications

An original Signature grasshopper design with hinged pallets on jewelled hinge pins and a light, open escape wheel, made to run dry for long periods. The pallets are shaped to kick the wheel forward at each beat, and the hinges are adjustable for kick length. This is a Signature original, labelled signature-original.

Mechanism

Each pallet hinges as the pendulum swings, its catch releases a tooth, and the opposite pallet kicks the wheel forward, hopping it from tooth to tooth. Because the pallets kick rather than drag, friction is low and the escapement runs with almost no oil. The adjustable hinges let the kick be tuned without recutting the wheel.

Maintenance

Run the pallets dry, keep the hinge pins clean, and check hinge shake at every service, because a loose hinge shortens the kick. Never oil the kicking faces, and never bend a pallet to adjust the kick; use the hinge adjustment.

Build and restoration guidance

Build the hinges with jewelled pins, set the kick so each pallet hands over cleanly, and test over days, because this design's accuracy shows in long runs. Keep a record of the hinge setting for the next service.

Tools

Jewelled hinge pins, fine files, timing machine, and a long test stand.

title: Signature Twin-Arm Gravity Escapement
body:
Specifications

An original Signature gravity design with two balanced gravity arms and a three-legged escape wheel, sized for a longcase clock rather than a turret clock. Each arm weighs the same, is pivoted on a jewel, and falls the same distance, so the pendulum receives an equal push on both swings. This is a Signature original, labelled signature-original.

Mechanism

The wheel lifts each arm in turn, and the arm falls under its own weight, pushing the pendulum with a fixed force that does not depend on the drive. Because the push comes from gravity, changes in the driving weight or spring do not reach the pendulum. The two arms alternate, so the pendulum is pushed on every swing.

Maintenance

Keep the lifting surfaces clean and dry, oil only the arm pivots, and check that both arms lift to the same height. A sticking arm makes the rate step, and the cure is cleaning the pivot, never adding weight to the arm.

Build and restoration guidance

Balance both arms on a jig before fitting, set their fall to contact the crutch squarely, and test with a heavy pendulum, because a light pendulum lets the arms disturb it. Record the arm weights in the service notes.

Tools

Arm balancing jig, clock oil, spirit level, and a heavy test pendulum.

title: Signature Single-Arm Gravity Escapement
body:
Specifications

An original Signature gravity design with one gravity arm and a wheel with teeth in two planes, made for smaller clocks where a twin-arm design would not fit. The single arm is counterweighted so its fall is repeatable, and it pushes the pendulum once per full oscillation. This is a Signature original, labelled signature-original.

Mechanism

The wheel lifts the arm as it turns, and the arm falls and pushes the pendulum with a fixed force. On the return swing the arm is lifted again without pushing, so the pendulum is driven once per cycle rather than once per beat. The single arm keeps the movement compact while preserving the gravity principle.

Maintenance

Keep the lifting surface clean and dry, oil the arm pivot only, and check the counterweight at every service. A single-arm clock that loses time in steps usually has a sticking pivot or a worn counterweight screw.

Build and restoration guidance

Build the arm with its counterweight adjustable, set the fall so it meets the crutch squarely, and test the rate over a week, because single-arm gravity clocks show their faults slowly. Do not file the wheel teeth to cure a sticking arm.

Tools

Arm balance, fine files, clock oil, and a timing reference.

title: Signature Pin-Wheel Clock Escapement
body:
Specifications

An original Signature pin-wheel design with a wheel carrying two rows of polished steel pins and simple steel pallets, made for a robust longcase movement. The pins are pressed into a brass wheel rim and stand at a fixed height, so the escapement tolerates small cutting errors. This is a Signature original, labelled signature-original.

Mechanism

Each pin meets a pallet, locks, and slides across the impulse face to push the pendulum, alternating between the two rows of pins. The round pins give a smooth action, and the simple pallets are easy to replace. Because the pins, not teeth, do the work, wear shows as a loose pin rather than a broken tooth, which is easier to repair.

Maintenance

Oil the pin contacts sparingly and check every pin for tightness at each service. A regular double beat points to one bent pin; straighten it only with the wheel supported, never by levering against the rim.

Build and restoration guidance

Replace loose pins with new ones pressed to the same height, set the pallet depth so each pin clears cleanly after impulse, and test the beat on both pallets before closing the movement.

Tools

Pin punches, staking tool, clock oil, loupe, and a beat tester.

title: Signature Spring Detent Clock Escapement
body:
Specifications

An original Signature detent design with a thin spring detent and a jewelled impulse pallet, made for a precision pendulum clock. The detent spring is cut from a single strip of spring steel and its tension is set by a screw, so the unlocking force can be tuned. This is a Signature original, labelled signature-original.

Mechanism

The detent stone locks the escape wheel until the pendulum's discharging pallet pushes the spring aside, freeing one tooth and giving impulse through the impulse pallet. On the return swing the discharging pallet passes without unlocking, because the spring flexes out of the way. The pendulum is therefore disturbed only at the moment of impulse.

Maintenance

Keep the detent spring dry and free of kinks, never oil it, and check the locking stone for chips at every service. A detent that gains suddenly has usually lost its lock, and the locking depth should be checked before the regulation is touched.

Build and restoration guidance

Set the locking depth so the wheel cannot creep, set the unlocking clearance so the pendulum just trips the detent, and test at full arc and low arc, because the detent must unlock reliably at both. Record the spring tension screw setting.

Tools

Detent spring stock, fine tweezers, loupe, clock oil for pivots only, and a timing machine.

title: Signature Pivoted Detent Clock Escapement
body:
Specifications

An original Signature pivoted detent design with the detent rocking on a jewelled arbor and a light return spring, made for a precision regulator clock. The pivoted form gives a crisp lock and unlock, and the return spring tension is adjustable. This is a Signature original, labelled signature-original.

Mechanism

The detent rocks on its arbor to lock the wheel, the pendulum's discharging pallet lifts it clear, the wheel escapes one tooth and gives impulse, and the return spring snaps the detent back to lock. Because the detent pivots rather than flexes, its action is repeatable over long service, provided its pivots stay in perfect condition.

Maintenance

Oil the detent pivots with one microscopic drop, keep the locking stone clean, and check the return spring at every service. A sticking detent either stops the clock or lets the wheel run, and both faults point to the pivots first.

Build and restoration guidance

Re-bush the detent pivots at the first sign of shake, set the lock so the tooth sits squarely on the stone, and adjust the banking screws rather than bending the detent arm. Test the lock at full and low arc.

Tools

Pivot polishers, bushing tools, clock oil, loupe, and timing machine.

title: Signature Cylinder Clock Escapement
body:
Specifications

An original Signature cylinder design with a hardened steel cylinder on the oscillator staff and an escape wheel with 15 teeth, made for a small teaching clock. The cylinder is polished inside and out, and its diameter is matched to the tooth spacing at build time. This is a Signature original, labelled signature-original.

Mechanism

A tooth enters the cylinder, rests on its inner wall while the oscillator swings, and escapes from the cylinder's edge, giving the push as it leaves. The tooth stays in contact for most of the swing, which makes this design simple and robust but sensitive to oil condition, and it is offered as a teaching escapement rather than a regulator.

Maintenance

Oil the cylinder and pivots with good clock oil and renew it at every service, because dried oil slows the oscillator quickly. Check the cylinder for cracks and the teeth for wear flats, and never thin the cylinder wall when polishing.

Build and restoration guidance

Match the cylinder diameter to the tooth spacing exactly before fitting, polish the acting surfaces lightly, and test the rate before and after oiling, so the owner can see the oil's effect. Record the cylinder diameter in the service notes.

Tools

Cylinder gauges, pivot polishers, clock oil, loupe, and an oscillator tester.

title: Signature Duplex Clock Escapement
body:
Specifications

An original Signature duplex design with long locking teeth and short impulse teeth on one wheel, and a locking roller plus impulse pallet on the oscillator staff, made for a portable teaching clock. The two tooth sets are cut on one wheel to keep the movement compact. This is a Signature original, labelled signature-original.

Mechanism

A long tooth rests on the locking roller while the oscillator swings freely, then the impulse pallet meets a short tooth and receives the push. Because the oscillator is free for most of its swing, this design is more accurate than the cylinder, though it is delicate and must be protected from shocks.

Maintenance

Keep the movement clean, oil the pivots only, and protect it from shocks, which can bend the impulse pallet or break a tooth. A duplex that stops when carried but runs on a table usually has a bent tooth or a loose impulse jewel.

Build and restoration guidance

Check every long tooth for straightness and every short tooth for height, set the locking roller so the long teeth clear it by the smallest safe margin, and never force the oscillator to test the lock.

Tools

Fine files, staking tool, clock oil, loupe, and a timing machine.

title: Signature Lever Clock Escapement
body:
Specifications

An original Signature lever design for platform-escapement clocks, with a lever fork, guard pin, and safety roller, and pallets faced in polished steel. It is self-starting and robust, and it is sized for a mantel clock with a balance rather than a pendulum. This is a Signature original, labelled signature-original.

Mechanism

The escape wheel drives the lever pallets, the lever fork engages the pin on the balance staff, and the lever gives the balance its impulse at each swing. The guard pin and safety roller stop the fork from jamming if the clock is knocked. The balance swings freely between impulses, which keeps the rate steady for an everyday clock.

Maintenance

Oil the pallet stones and pivots sparingly, keep the hairspring free of oil, and check the banking pins at every service. A loud, uneven tick usually means a bent lever or a loose pallet stone, not a faulty balance.

Build and restoration guidance

Level the pallets, set equal lock and drop, adjust the banking pins so the lever throws fully without overbanking, and test the draw before closing the movement. Record the banking setting in the service notes.

Tools

Lever setting tools, pallet setters, clock oil, loupe, and a timing machine.

title: Signature Pulse Toggle Clock Escapement
body:
Specifications

An original Signature electrically maintained pendulum escapement, in which a small electromagnet pushes the pendulum only when its arc falls below a set point, and a toggle contact controls the pulse. The design is made for a master clock driving slave dials, and it uses a low-voltage supply. This is a Signature original, labelled signature-original.

Mechanism

The pendulum swings freely for many beats, and when its arc drops, the toggle trips, current flows through the magnet, the armature pushes the pendulum, and the toggle resets. The current then switches off, and the pendulum swings freely again. Slave dials are stepped by the master's contacts, so one master can run a building's clocks.

Maintenance

Keep the contacts clean and correctly gapped, check the supply voltage, and keep the toggle mechanism free of oil where the design runs dry. A falling arc with a good supply usually means dirty contacts, not a weak magnet.

Build and restoration guidance

Set the contact gap so the impulse fires at the right arc, check the magnet's pull separately from the slave circuit, and never bridge the contacts while the pendulum swings, because the magnet can grab the armature and stop the clock.

Tools

Contact burnisher, multimeter, screwdrivers, clock oil for pivots, and a test battery.

title: Signature Remontoir Clock Escapement
body:
Specifications

An original Signature constant-force design with a small remontoir spring rewound by the going train every fifteen seconds, so the escapement always receives the same force. The remontoir spring is housed in its own barrel, and the rewinding is done through a separate wheel that does not disturb the escapement. This is a Signature original, labelled signature-original.

Mechanism

The going train winds the remontoir spring a little at fixed intervals, and the remontoir spring alone drives the escape wheel, so its force stays nearly constant through each cycle. The pendulum therefore receives the same impulse at every beat, no matter how the main driving weight or spring varies. The rewinding interval is short, so the force never drifts far.

Maintenance

Service the remontoir spring and its winding mechanism at every overhaul, and check that rewinding happens at regular intervals. A remontoir that rewinds unevenly makes the rate step up and down, and the fault is usually in the winding wheel, not the escapement.

Build and restoration guidance

Match the winding interval and spring strength to the escapement's power needs with a safety margin, and test the force at the escape wheel over a full winding cycle before fitting the pendulum. Record the spring strength and interval in the service notes.

Tools

Spring winders, force gauge, clock oil, timing machine, and a test stand.

title: Signature Brocot-Style Adjustable Escapement
body:
Specifications

An original Signature adjustable deadbeat design with pallets mounted in the anchor arms on screws, so lock and drop can be set without recutting the wheel. The escape wheel is light and open, and the pallets are faced in polished steel. This is a Signature original, labelled signature-original, inspired by the adjustable-pallet idea rather than copied from any maker.

Mechanism

A tooth locks on a pallet's locking face while the pendulum swings freely, then slides onto the impulse face to give the push, on the deadbeat principle. The screw-mounted pallets let the repairer set the lock and drop in tiny steps, which makes this design easy to maintain far from a workshop. The light wheel keeps the pendulum's swing undisturbed.

Maintenance

Adjust the pallets in tiny steps, check the lock after each move, and lock the adjusting screws firmly when the drop is equal. Oil the impulse faces sparingly, and never adjust one pallet without checking the other.

Build and restoration guidance

Keep the original adjustable pallets if they are sound, set the anchor so the pallets engage symmetrically, and polish only the impulse faces. Test at a small arc, where this design is at its best.

Tools

Small screwdrivers, pallet adjusting tool, clock oil, loupe, and timing machine.

title: Signature Verge-Balance Teaching Escapement
body:
Specifications

An original Signature teaching escapement that pairs a crown wheel and verge with a balance wheel and hairspring, sized for a demonstration clock with a visible movement. The balance is large, so its swing is easy to see, and the crown wheel is open, so each tooth's escape is visible. This is a Signature original, labelled signature-original.

Mechanism

Each swing of the balance rocks the verge, one pallet releases a crown-wheel tooth while the other drops onto the next, and the hairspring returns the balance with a small push from the escapement each swing. The large balance makes the action slow enough to follow by eye, which is the point of the teaching design.

Maintenance

Oil the balance pivots and pallet faces sparingly, keep the hairspring free of oil and distortion, and check the banking so the balance swings freely. A hairspring touching its coils will ruin the rate and is visible before it is audible.

Build and restoration guidance

Keep the crown wheel, verge, and balance as a matched set, test the balance for poise before fitting the hairspring, and set the banking so the balance never hits the cock. Demonstrate the escapement at slow speed before running it at full rate.

Tools

Balance poising tool, hairspring tweezers, clock oil, pegwood, and a loupe.
